questions.answer: (a) They were novelists. The best known novelists in the nineteenth century were the Bronte sisters. Their writings became important in defining a new type of women.

questions.text: Mention the three types of flows within international economic exchanges during the 19th century.
questions.answer:
The three types of flows were:
a. Flow of Trade: trade in goods like wheat, cotton, etc. (e.g. Indian fine cotton cloth exports fell after industrialisation in Europe and tariff barriers; India began exporting raw cotton and importing mill-made cloth from England).
b. Flow of Labour: migration of people in search of employment. Nearly 50 million people emigrated from Europe to America and Australia in the 19th century; about 150 million people worldwide left their homes in search of a better future.
c. Flow of Capital Investment: long-term or short-term investments over long distances. Capital flowed from financial centres such as London to build railways and other projects.

or.text: Explain the role of New International Economic Order (NIEO).
or.answer: G-77 (Group of 77) demanded a New International Economic Order (NIEO), a system that would give them: a. real control over their own natural resources; b. more development assistance from advanced/western countries; c. fairer prices for raw materials and better access for their manufactured goods in developed countries' markets.

questions.text: The Non-Cooperation Movement became wider with the integration of the Awadh Peasants Struggle. Explain the statement with three arguments.
questions.answer:
The Non-Cooperation Movement drew into its fold the struggles of peasants and tribals. It became wider with the integration of the Awadh Peasants Struggle:
- In Awadh, peasants were led by Baba Ramchandra; the movement was against talukdars and landlords. Peasants had to do begar and had no right over the leased land.
- The peasant movement demanded a reduction of revenue. Nai-dhobi bandhs were organised. The Oudh Kisan Sabha was set up, headed by Jawaharlal Nehru and Baba Ramchandra.
- This Awadh peasant struggle was integrated with the Non-Cooperation Movement into the wider struggle.

or.text: The effects of Non-Cooperation Movement on the economic front were more dramatic. Support the statement with examples.
or.answer:
- Foreign goods were boycotted, liquor shops picketed, and foreign cloth burnt in huge bonfires.
- The import of foreign cloth halved between 1921 and 1922, its value dropping from Rs 102 crore to Rs 57 crore.
- In many places merchants and traders refused to trade in foreign goods or finance foreign trade.
- As the boycott spread, people discarded imported clothes and wore only Indian ones; production of Indian textile mills and handlooms went up.

questions.text: "The use of Polish language came to be seen as a symbol of the struggle against Russian dominance". Justify the statement.
questions.answer: Language played an important role in developing nationalist sentiments. After Russian occupation, the Polish language was forced out of schools and the Russian language was imposed everywhere. In 1831, an armed rebellion against Russian rule took place which was ultimately crushed. Following this, many members of the clergy in Poland began to use language as a weapon of national resistance. Polish was used for church gatherings and all religious instruction. As a result, a large number of priests and bishops were put in jail or sent to Siberia by the Russian authorities as punishment for their refusal to preach in Russian. So the use of Polish came to be seen as a symbol of the struggle against Russian dominance.

or.text: How did culture play an important role in Europe in creating the idea of the nation?
or.answer:
i. Art, music, literature and drama helped to express, shape and strengthen nationalist sentiments.
ii. Romantics like the German philosopher Johann Gottfried Herder held that true German culture could be discovered only among the common people, the das Volk.
iii. The glorification of reason and science was criticised by the romantic artists; they favoured emotions, intuitions and mystical feelings.
iv. Language too boosted nationalism: the Poles used Polish in church gatherings and religious instruction against Russian occupation and the ban on Polish.
v. The Grimm Brothers used German stories and folktales to promote the German spirit against French domination.
vi. Operas and music, like that of Karol Kurpinski, kept alive the national spirit.
vii. Folk dances like the polonaise and mazurka became national symbols.

questions.text:
Read the following text carefully and answer the questions that follow:
The lives and feelings of women began to be written in particularly vivid and intense ways. Women's reading, therefore, increased enormously in middle-class homes. Liberal husbands and fathers began educating their womenfolk at home and sent them to schools when women's schools were set up in the cities and towns after the mid-nineteenth century. Many journals began carrying writings by women and explained why women should be educated. They also carried a syllabus and attached suitable reading matter which could be used for home-based schooling.
But not all families were liberal. Conservative Hindus believed that a literate girl would be widowed and Muslims feared that educated women would be corrupted by reading Urdu romances. Sometimes, rebel women defied such prohibition. We know the story of a girl in a conservative Muslim family of north India who secretly learnt to read and write in Urdu. Her family wanted her to read only the Arabic Quran which she did not understand. So she insisted on learning to read a language that was her own. In East Bengal, in the early nineteenth century, Rashsundari Debi, a young married girl in a very orthodox household, learnt to read in the secrecy of her kitchen. Later, she wrote her autobiography Amar Jiban which was published in 1876. It was the first full-length autobiography published in the Bengali language.

subparts.text: Give the contribution of journals in bringing awareness for women's education?
subparts.answer: Many journals began carrying writings by women and explained why women should be educated. They also carried a syllabus and attached suitable reading matter which could be used for home-based schooling.

subparts.answer:

questions.text: Enlist the various institutional reforms programmes introduced by the government in the interest of the farmers.
questions.answer:
a. Establishment of the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR), agricultural universities and animal breeding centres for research and development in agriculture.
b. Investment in rural infrastructure to link the rural market with the international market.

questions.text:
Study the given flow chart and answer the question that follows:
Explain the added value product in the textile industry on the bases of above flowchart.
questions.answer: Cotton undergoes several stages of value addition before reaching consumers as finished garments. After harvesting, cotton is processed to remove seeds and impurities, producing raw fibre. This fibre is spun into yarn using various spinning techniques, preparing it for weaving or knitting. The yarn is transformed into fabric, a more functional and versatile material. The fabric then undergoes dyeing, printing and finishing to improve appearance, texture and durability. The finished fabric is cut, stitched and tailored into garments such as shirts, dresses or jeans. Throughout this chain the industry creates value at each stage and supports allied industries such as chemicals, dyes, machinery and packaging.

or.text: Why does the textile industry occupy an important position in the Indian economy? Explain.
or.answer:
- It accounts for 14% of industrial production.
- It provides jobs to 35 million people, a major employment sector.
- It contributes about 24.6% of India's foreign exchange earnings.
- It contributes 4% to the country's GDP.
- It is the only industry in India that is entirely self-reliant.
- It is the only industry that is complete in the value chain, from raw material to the highest value-added products.

questions.text:
Read the following text carefully and answer the questions that follow:
CONSERVATION OF ENERGY RESOURCES
Energy is a basic requirement for economic development. Every sector of the national economy - agriculture, industry, transport, commercial and domestic - needs inputs of energy. The economic development plans implemented since independence necessarily required increasing amounts of energy to remain operational. As a result, consumption of energy in all forms has been steadily rising all over the country. In this background, there is an urgent need to develop a sustainable path of energy development. Promotion of energy conservation and increased use of renewable energy sources are the twin planks of sustainable energy. India is presently one of the least energy efficient countries in the world. We have to adopt a cautious approach for the judicious use of our limited energy resources. For example, as concerned citizens we can do our bit by using public transport systems instead of individual vehicles; switching off electricity when not in use, using power-saving devices and using non-conventional sources of energy. At last "Energy Saved is energy produced"

subparts.text: Why is sustainable energy a key to sustainable development?
subparts.answer: Sustainable energy ensures that current energy needs are met without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs, promoting long-term economic growth and environmental preservation.

subparts.text: Why is consumption of energy rising in all over India?
subparts.answer: Because the economic development plans implemented since independence demand increasing energy inputs in every sector - agriculture, industry, transport, commercial and domestic.

subparts.text: Explain Energy saved is energy produced.
subparts.answer: It stresses energy conservation: reducing wastage and using energy efficiently effectively creates additional energy resources without raising production. Using public transport, switching off lights when not in use and using power-saving devices conserve energy, making it available for other purposes - energy that would otherwise be wasted.

questions.text:

questions.text:

options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.answer: (d) A is false but R is true. There is overwhelming support for democracy all over the world because it is an accountable, responsive and legitimate government.

questions.text: Describe any three features of federal government.
questions.answer:
i. Power is divided between the central authority and its various constituent units.
ii. All levels of governance govern the same citizens, but their jurisdiction is different.
iii. Any change in the fundamental provisions of the Constitution has to be passed by both houses of Parliament and then ratified by the legislatures of at least half the number of states.

questions.text: Describe any two provisions made in the Constitution to establish the model of 'secular governance' in India.
questions.answer:
i. The Constitution provides all individuals and communities the freedom to profess, practise and propagate any religion, or not to follow any.
ii. The Constitution allows the state to intervene in matters of religion to ensure equality within religious communities, e.g. it bans untouchability.

questions.text: How does democracy establish an accountable, responsible and legitimate governance? Explain.
questions.answer:
i. People have the right to choose their rulers and have control over the rulers.
ii. Citizens can participate in decision-making so that the government is accountable to them.
iii. Decision-making is based on norms and procedures.
iv. A democratic government is legitimate: it may be slow, less efficient, not always responsive or clean, but it is the people's own government.

questions.text: Define the term Political Party. Explain with examples, the need of political parties in India.
questions.answer:
A political party is a group of people who come together to contest elections and hold power in the government. The necessity of parties can be understood by imagining a situation without them:
i. Every candidate in elections would be independent, so no one could make promises to the people about major policy changes.
ii. Elected representatives would be accountable to their constituency for local work, but no one would be responsible for how the country is run.
iii. The rise of parties is linked to the emergence of representative democracies; as societies became large and complex they needed an agency to gather different views and present them to the government.
iv. They were needed to bring various representatives together so that a responsible government could be formed.
v. They provide a mechanism to support or restrain the government, make policies, and justify or oppose them.

or.text: Explain the meaning of a Political Party. Mention its components. Name any two recognized national parties in India.
or.answer:
A political party is a group of people that come together to contest elections and hold power in the government. They agree on some policies and programmes for the society with a view to promote the collective good. Since there can be different views on what is good for all, parties try to persuade people why their policies are better and seek to implement them by winning popular support through elections.
Components: A. the leaders; B. the active members; C. the followers.
Two recognised national parties: Bharatiya Janata Party; Indian National Congress.

questions.text:
Read the following text carefully and answer the questions that follow:
Two different sets of reasons can be given in favour of power-sharing. Firstly, power-sharing is good because it helps to reduce the possibility of conflict between social groups. Since social conflict often leads to violence and political instability, power-sharing is a good way to ensure the stability of political order. Imposing the will of the majority community over others may look like an attractive option in the short run, but in the long run, it undermines the unity of the nation. The tyranny of the majority is not just oppressive for the minority; it often brings ruin to the majority as well. There is a second, deeper reason why power sharing is good for democracies. Power-sharing is the very spirit of democracy. A democratic rule involves sharing power with those affected by its exercise, and who have to live with its effects. People have a right to be consulted on how they are to be governed. A legitimate government is one where citizens, through participation, acquire a stake in the system. The first set of reasons is Prudential and the second is moral. While prudential reasons stress that power-sharing will bring out better outcomes, the former emphasises the very act of powersharing as valuable.

subparts.text: What is the essence of a legitimate government in a democracy?
subparts.answer: A legitimate government is one where citizens, through participation and consultation on how they are governed, acquire a stake in the system.

subparts.text: What is the downside of imposing the will of the majority community over others?
subparts.answer: It leads to the tyranny of the majority, which is oppressive for the minority and often ruins the majority as well; it undermines national unity in the long run.

subparts.text: How does power-sharing contribute to the stability of political order?
subparts.answer: Power-sharing helps to reduce the possibility of conflict between social groups. Since social conflict often leads to violence and political instability, power-sharing is a good way to ensure the stability of political order.

questions.text: Workers are exploited in the unorganised sector. Do you agree with this view? Give reasons in support of your answer.
questions.answer:
Yes, workers are exploited in the unorganised sector:
i. It is characterised by small and scattered units largely outside government control.
ii. There are rules and regulations but they are not followed.
iii. Jobs are low-paid and often not regular.
iv. There is no provision for overtime, paid leave, holidays or leave due to sickness.
v. Employment is not secure; people can be asked to leave without any reason.
vi. On retirement there is no pension or provident fund.

questions.text: Manav needs a loan to set-up a small business. On what basis will Manav decide whether to borrow from the bank or the moneylender? Discuss.
questions.answer:
Manav will decide on the basis of the loan terms:
i. The collateral and documentation required - he should be able to provide these.
ii. The difference between the rates of interest charged by formal and informal sources.
iii. The mode of repayment - size of instalment, frequency (monthly, quarterly, half-yearly, annually) or full repayment at the end of a period.
iv. His own capacity to repay after analysing the information collected, and the penalty in case of default.

questions.text: Should more Indian companies emerge as MNCs? How would it benefit the people in the country?
questions.answer:
Yes, more Indian companies should emerge as MNCs because:
i. New job opportunities would be created and the Indian economy would improve.
ii. Local companies would supply raw materials and other services to them and prosper.
iii. It would raise production standards and improve the standard of living of the people.
iv. MNCs produce on a large scale at lower costs and earn profits; India could spread its production across the globe and dominate international markets. As exports increase, the balance of trade would become favourable.

questions.text: Explain any five differences between public and private sectors.
questions.answer:
| Basis | Public Sector | Private Sector |
|---|---|---|
| Ownership | Most assets are owned by the government. | Most assets are owned by individuals or groups of individuals. |
| Service provision | The government provides services. | Services are provided by private owners. |
| Funding | The government raises money for various activities through taxes. | Private sector collects money through the services it provides. |
| Profit motive | Activities are focused on public welfare, not just profit. | Activities are guided by the motive to earn profits. |
| Examples | Railways, Post Office, etc. | Tata Steel, Reliance, etc. |

or.text: Define the term unorganised sector. Explain any the reasons why people like to work in the organised sector.
or.answer:
The unorganised sector includes small and scattered units which are largely outside government control. There are rules and regulations but they are not followed; jobs are low paid and irregular, and employment is not secure.
Reasons people prefer the organised sector:
i. Workers enjoy security of employment and work only a fixed number of hours.
ii. Enterprises are registered by the government and follow rules such as the Factories Act, Industrial Disputes Act, Minimum Wages Act, etc.
iii. Workers get paid leave, payment during holidays, provident fund, gratuity, pension on retirement, etc.
iv. Workers get medical benefits and facilities like a safe working environment and clean drinking water.
v. Terms of employment are regular; people have assured work.
